lead: Spread spectrum takes a narrowband data signal and deliberately spreads it over a far wider band with a fast pseudo-noise (PN) code that the receiver also knows. The receiver undoes the spreading for the wanted signal, while a jammer, an interferer or another user stays spread and mostly falls outside the data band. Direct sequence (DSSS) multiplies the data by the code; frequency hopping (FHSS) moves the carrier from channel to channel. GPS, CDMA mobile, Bluetooth and anti-jam military radios are built on these ideas.
prereq: You need: BPSK and the idea of autocorrelation (see signals, noise and random processes).

sections.h3: PN sequences, chips and processing gain

blocks.text: A PN sequence is a deterministic binary sequence that looks random. A shift register of m stages with exclusive-OR feedback makes one; when the feedback taps are chosen well, it runs through all 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 non-zero states before repeating, a maximal-length sequence (m-sequence). Each PN bit is called a chip, of length T<sub>c</sub>, and the chip rate R<sub>c</sub> = 1/T<sub>c</sub> is much higher than the bit rate.

This 3-stage register, started at 111, gives 1 1 1 0 0 1 0, period 2³ − 1 = 7. It shows the three m-sequence properties: balance (four 1s, three 0s), runs (half the runs have length 1, a quarter length 2, and so on) and a two-valued autocorrelation: in ±1 form the sequence agrees with itself in all 7 places at zero shift and gives −1 at every other shift. That sharp peak lets the receiver find the code phase.
the processing gain of DSSS, the number of chips per bit; in decibels G<sub>p</sub>(dB) = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(R<sub>c</sub>/R<sub>b</sub>). R<sub>c</sub> is in chips/s and R<sub>b</sub> in bit/s.

blocks.where: d(t) is the bipolar data (±1) at R<sub>b</sub> and c(t) the bipolar PN code (±1) at R<sub>c</sub>. The product d·c is a ±1 wave at the chip rate, so the BPSK signal now occupies about 2R<sub>c</sub> instead of 2R<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.text: The receiver multiplies by the same carrier and by the same code, aligned to the chip. Since c(t)² = 1 the data returns, and the correlator integrates over T<sub>b</sub> as for BPSK. With a different code, or the right code a chip out of step, the correlation is close to zero.

A narrowband jammer at the carrier meets the code only once, at the receiver, so the multiplication spreads it over about 2R<sub>c</sub>; the data filter then keeps only about 1/G<sub>p</sub> of its power. The jamming margin is how many dB the jammer power J may exceed the signal power S at the receiver input while the despread E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> still meets its target:
L<sub>sys</sub> is the implementation loss of the system, often taken as 0 in exam questions.

FHSS keeps a narrowband modulation (usually M-FSK) but the PN code drives a frequency synthesiser that picks one of N channels at each hop. The receiver's synthesiser follows the same pattern. If the hop band is W<sub>ss</sub> and each channel B wide, N = W<sub>ss</sub>/B and the processing gain is G<sub>p</sub> ≈ N.

items: Slow hopping: several symbols per hop (hop rate below the symbol rate); simple synthesiser, but a hit channel loses a burst of symbols.
Fast hopping: several hops per symbol; each symbol is spread over several channels, so a jammer on one channel spoils only part of it; needs a fast synthesiser and tight timing.

blocks.text: DSSS spreads every symbol over the whole band at once; FHSS occupies one channel at a time but visits the whole band over many hops. Code-division multiple access (CDMA) gives each user its own code. The receiver correlates with one code and the other users, having low cross-correlation, look like added noise. A strong nearby user can still swamp a distant one (the near-far problem), so CDMA needs tight power control.

examples.question: A DSSS link sends R<sub>b</sub> = 9.6 kb/s with a PN code at R<sub>c</sub> = 1.2288 Mchip/s. (a) Find G<sub>p</sub> as a ratio and in dB. (b) The demodulator needs E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 7 dB; find the jamming margin, ignoring losses, and say how much stronger than the signal a jammer may be.
steps: As a ratio 10<sup>1.407</sup> = 25.5: the jammer may be about 25 times stronger than the signal at the antenna.
examples.answer: G<sub>p</sub> = 128 (21.07 dB); M<sub>j</sub> = 14.07 dB, a jammer about 25.5 times the signal power.

examples.question: An FHSS radio sends 10 kb/s BFSK. It hops over a 25 MHz band in 25 kHz channels. Find the number of hop frequencies and the processing gain. For fast hopping at 4 hops per bit find the hop rate and dwell time; for slow hopping at 1000 hops/s find the bits per hop.
steps: Fast: hop rate = 4 × 10 000 = 40 000 hops/s; dwell = 1/40 000 = 25 µs per hop.
Slow: bits per hop = 10 000/1000 = 10 bits; dwell 1 ms.
examples.answer: 1000 hop frequencies, G<sub>p</sub> = 30 dB; fast hopping 40 khop/s with 25 µs dwell; slow hopping 10 bits per hop.

traps: The chip rate is not the bit rate: R<sub>c</sub> = G<sub>p</sub> × R<sub>b</sub>.
Gains in cascade multiply as ratios, which is the same as adding their dB values; never add the ratios themselves.

M<sub>j</sub> = G<sub>p</sub>(dB) − (E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)<sub>req</sub>(dB) − L<sub>sys</sub>; adding the required E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> instead of subtracting it is the common slip. The answer is a power ratio in dB, not watts.
Despreading needs the same code in step to within a fraction of a chip; a one-chip offset of an m-sequence gives a correlation of −1/N, almost nothing.
The chip-rate formula R<sub>c</sub>/R<sub>b</sub> is for DSSS. For FHSS the processing gain is the number of hop channels, W<sub>ss</sub>/B.

quiz.q: What is a chip, and what is the period of an m-sequence from m stages?
quiz.a: One bit of the PN code; 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 chips.

quiz.q: Why does a narrowband jammer lose most of its power in a DSSS receiver?
quiz.a: The receiver multiplies by the code, which despreads the wanted signal but spreads the jammer over about 2R<sub>c</sub>; the data filter keeps only about 1/G<sub>p</sub> of it.

quiz.q: R<sub>b</sub> = 20 kb/s and R<sub>c</sub> = 2.56 Mchip/s. Find G<sub>p</sub>.
G<sub>p</sub> = 1023 chips per bit and E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB is needed with 2 dB of losses. Find M<sub>j</sub>.
Bluetooth hops over 79 channels of 1 MHz at 1600 hops/s. Find G<sub>p</sub> and the dwell time.
The receiver code is right but half a chip late. What happens?
quiz.a: The correlation peak drops to about half, so the despread signal falls about 6 dB while the noise does not; the error rate rises. A tracking loop keeps the timing within a small fraction of a chip.

quiz.q: Compare slow and fast FHSS against a jammer that follows the hops.
quiz.a: Slow hopping stays on a channel long enough for a follower to find and jam it; fast hopping leaves before the jammer can react and spreads each symbol over several channels.

beyond: Not for the exam. GPS civil signals are DSSS with 1023-chip Gold codes at 1.023 Mchip/s; LoRa uses chirp spread spectrum; 3G was built on wideband CDMA. Research continues on multi-user detection, which cancels the other users instead of treating them as noise. Search next: Gold codes, rake receiver, multi-user detection.

spec.aria: Three square waves over 14 chip periods: the data, plus 1 for 7 chips then minus 1 for 7 chips; the code 1110010 repeated twice; and their product, which equals the code in the first bit and the inverted code in the second.
